explanation: An eclipsing binary with P = 9.057 d. TESS shows repeated, symmetric dips of about 8-9% (about 0.2 d long) that recur at that period across two years (1599.14, 1608.22, 1626.31, 1635.37, 2332.78 and later). Recurrence aligns 10 of 11 events with purity 1, and the strict-period test gives delta_bits 28. The two Gaia dips are single transits on different fields of view (fov 1 and 2), each about 5.5% deep and grey across G, BP and RP. That fits an occultation by a star seen part-way through the eclipse, not an artefact. The high RUWE (7.8) points to a companion, possibly a third body. No secondary eclipse is seen, so the system could be eccentric or have a faint secondary. A large-planet transit is less likely given the depth and the V-shaped profile.

The deepest dip (G 0.881 at t=469.5) is one flagged epoch with an error of 0.089, so it is only about 1.3 sigma. Its other field of view and BP/RP at the same time are normal (0.991/0.994), so it is a bad measurement and not a real dimming. The shallower dips (about 1.5% at t=19 and t=293) last for several transits and appear coherently in G, BP and RP. They match the slow 0.5-1.5% wander seen elsewhere (t=71, 88, 706), as expected from rotational spot modulation. The ZTF single-epoch outliers do not recur, and recurrence/strict_period find no period. Nothing points to eclipses or anything unexplained.

explanation: A long-period detached eclipsing binary (P ~ 63.87 d). Recurrence puts all 30 events from Gaia and ZTF into one pure primary window (aligned_fraction 1, purity 1, delta_bits 183), which only strict periodic eclipses do. ZTF shows flat floors at about 0.064 in g and 0.16 in r/i, repeated across several events. This points to a total eclipse of the hotter star, with a cooler, larger companion left visible and redder. Gaia catches only partial phases (ingress or egress, about 1 d long, nearly grey in BP/RP), seen in both fields of view, with no scan-angle or coincidence signature. The totality lasting more than 1 d at a 64 d period needs a large (sub)giant eclipser. The star is quiet otherwise, and TESS sectors fell outside the eclipses.

The second 'dip' at t=0 is another flagged epoch with a small fov offset against its pair. TESS shows no comparable events. p_eb is tiny with 127 expected repeats, so a periodic eclipse is unlikely. The likeliest cause is a defective or gated G measurement. A minor blend contribution is possible because RUWE is 3.45, which suggests a companion.

explanation: This is the catalogued EA eclipsing binary (P = 7.59 d). The two dips at t = 127.55 and 317.28 are 189.73 d apart, which is 25.00 cycles. They fall at the same phase within 0.001 (catalogue_ephemeris: 2 of 2 on ephemeris). Both dips have the same depth (about 9.4% and 9.1%, depth CV 0.018) and the same depth in G, BP and RP, so the occulter is grey, as one star eclipsing another would be. The 127.48 epoch, at 2% depth, catches ingress 106.5 min before the deeper point. That matches an eclipse a few hours long. Each dip shows in both FOV-2 transits and in all three bands, which argues against a detector or FOV artefact. RUWE is 1.03 and nothing else is blended. The non-testable recurrence statistic only reflects that there are just two events.

The primary and secondary eclipses are both about 40% deep. The dips are grey and of equal depth in BP, RP, G and ZTF g/r/i, which is what an eclipse by a stellar companion produces. Within the 106.5 min FoV pairs the flux changes quickly (0.57 to 0.88), which fits eclipse ingress and egress lasting hours at a 2 d period. They are seen in both fields of view, the coincidence and solar-system tests are clear, and ruwe is about 1. The catalogue SR label at 75.9 d is probably a misclassification or an alias: only 34 of 145 events fall on that ephemeris.

The dips are grey in BP and RP, are seen in both fields of view, and RUWE, BP/RP excess and blending flags are all clean. TESS contamination is only 4%, so dilution or a blend would hardly change the depths. A secondary eclipse this deep rules out a planet.

That combination (point-like, zero parallax, blue optical plus red near-IR, aperiodic red-noise variability of tens of per cent) is the signature of a quasar/AGN. TESS is useless (contamination 157).

explanation: An RS CVn star (catalogue period 52.5 d) whose G, BP and RP all vary together by about +-6-10%, as spots do. The pipeline's own test finds no period, and only one other dip event.

explanation: The dip is one G epoch (t=306.724, flux 0.924) with an error of 0.067, about 80 times the typical 0.0008. That makes it only about a 1.1 sigma deviation by its own error bar. That error points to disagreement between the per-CCD fluxes in that transit: a cosmic ray, a bad CCD or window problem, or a partly rejected transit. BP and RP taken at the same moment are normal (1.005 and 0.997), and so is the other field of view's G only 0.074 d later (1.0025). explanation: A detached eclipsing binary with P = 3.109 d. The recurrence test puts 40 of 46 events across Gaia, ZTF and TESS into one pure phase window (purity 1.0, delta_bits 297, p_random about 4e-90). TESS shows repeated dips of about 12%, each about 0.15 d long and spaced about 3.1 d apart. The Gaia dips are grey in BP and RP and are seen in both fields of view (at 760.91 and 760.98), which rules out a one-transit artefact. A depth of about 12% with no secondary eclipse and a short duration fits a low-mass stellar companion, or an equal-mass pair at twice the period. It is too deep for a planet around a star of this colour. The few non-aligned ZTF events (0.16, 0.66) look like bad single epochs.
